hints: Start by looking at chromosome position - are chromosomes lined up together in the middle of the cell or are they being pulled apart toward the poles?
Think about what makes meiosis I special - when do you still see maternal and paternal homologues together in the same cell, and when have they already been separated?
Recall when crossing over can happen - it needs homologous chromosomes to be closely paired with chiasmata visible, so which single diagram shows paired homologues touching and exchanging segments?
Count chromosome sets to judge ploidy - after the first nuclear division the cells have only one chromosome from each homologous pair, so which diagrams are after that separation?
walkthrough:
Spot anaphase by movement to poles**
Chromosomes being pulled apart on spindle fibres toward opposite poles means anaphase. In K, whole chromosomes (each still made of two chromatids) are moving apart in a single cell - that is anaphase I. In M, there are two cells side by side and in each cell chromatids are moving apart - that is anaphase II. So anaphase is K and M.

Find where homologues are still together**
A diploid pollen mother cell starts with pairs of homologous chromosomes, one dark and one light in the diagram. In J the homologues are paired as bivalents on the metaphase I plate. In K they are still in the same cell, just separating. After the first division the homologues are in different cells. So pairs of homologues in the same cell are J and K only.

Place crossing over in prophase I**
Crossing over is the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes when they synapse. It is visible as chromosomes touching and overlapping. Only J shows bivalents paired on the equator with overlapping chromatids where exchange occurs. K, L, M and N are already separating or separated, so crossing over is J.

Decide haploid versus diploid**
Haploid means one set of chromosomes, no homologous pairs. Meiosis I is reduction division, so after K the two daughter cells each receive only one homologue from each pair. L shows two cells after meiosis I, M shows those two cells in second division, and N shows the four products (tetrad of pollen grains). All of L, M and N are haploid.
Final answer: anaphase: K and M; cells containing pairs of homologous chromosomes: J and K; crossing over: J; haploid cells: L and M and N.

hints: Think about what the tassels produce and what would happen if they were left on the plant during flowering.
Think about what an F1 hybrid must be - offspring of two different selected parents - and what role the detasselled plant can then only play.
walkthrough:
Why male parts are a problem**
Maize has male and female flowers on the same plant, so its own pollen could easily land on its own female silks. That self-pollination would give inbred seed, not a hybrid. Removing the tassels removes the source of its own pollen.

How this guarantees a true F1**
With no anthers, the plant cannot pollinate itself and can only receive pollen. The breeder then dusts on pollen from a different, specially chosen variety. All seeds formed are therefore cross-pollinated hybrids between the two selected parents, with the detasselled plant acting as the female parent.

Final answer: Remove tassels (male anthers) to prevent self-pollination and ensure cross-pollination; pollen must come from a different selected parent plant, so the detasselled plant acts only as the female parent.

hints: Break the process into two stages - first create pure-breeding lines, then cross them - and think what the first stage aims to fix.
Think about what repeated self-pollination or crossing of close relatives over many generations does to homozygosity.
Think about how breeders keep only plants showing traits like disease resistance, rapid growth or high yield each generation.
Think about what happens when you cross two different homozygous lines - why all F1 offspring look the same and grow vigorously.
walkthrough:
Stage 1 - Make homozygous inbred lines**
Start with plants showing a useful trait and inbreed them, in maize usually by self-pollination or crossing close relatives. Each generation select the best offspring showing the desired trait, e.g. disease resistance, rapid growth or high yield, and breed them together again.

Why repeated selection fixes alleles**
Repeated inbreeding increases homozygosity because the same alleles are brought together generation after generation. After many cycles you get a pure-breeding line that is homozygous at most loci and always passes on the same alleles, but it is often less vigorous due to inbreeding depression.

Stage 2 - Cross two different lines**
Take two different inbred lines that each carry different desirable traits and cross-pollinate them (outcross / hybridise). For example, one line resistant to disease crossed with another line giving high yield.

Why the F1 is vigorous and uniform**
All F1 offspring receive the same combination of alleles - one set from each homozygous parent - so they are genetically very similar and therefore uniform in phenotype. They are heterozygous at many loci, which masks deleterious recessive alleles and gives heterosis or hybrid vigour: fast, healthy growth and high productivity.

Final answer: Stage 1: inbreed by repeated self-pollination / line breeding, selecting for desired traits such as disease resistance, rapid growth, high yield each generation to produce homozygous pure lines. Stage 2: outcross / hybridise two different pure lines with different desired traits to produce heterozygous F1 offspring that are uniform and show hybrid vigour.
